strengths: Principled and statistically rigorous framework: The paper successfully marries prediction-powered inference (PPI) with sequential testing / anytime-valid confidence sequences (SRM) to enable semi-supervised model risk monitoring. It guarantees finite-sample, assumption-free type-I error control regardless of the quality or calibration of the auxiliary predictor.

Adaptive weighting mechanism: The derivation and use of an online, predictable estimator for the weighting parameter $\eta_t$ ensures validity while effectively minimizing estimator variance. The authors also clearly articulate the trade-off between variance reduction and the range-normalization penalty in Appendix A.4 (Proposition A.1).

Diverse and realistic experimental validation: The method is evaluated across diverse domains, including vision (CIFAR-10-C), modern LLM question-answering with various auxiliary judge models (Qwen, GPT-4), and telecommunications channel equalization. Both abrupt and gradual shifts, as well as intermittent labeling streams, are thoroughly explored.
High presentation quality: The paper is well-written, clearly organized, and the problem setting, notation, and algorithmic details are easy to follow.
weaknesses: Incremental algorithmic novelty: The proposed framework is essentially a direct combination of existing tools—specifically, applying PPI++ estimators within the sequential risk monitoring (SRM) framework using conjugate-mixture empirical Bernstein bounds (Howard et al., 2021).

Modest practical detection gains in some setups: Because prediction-powered estimates expand the support to $[-\eta, 1+\eta]$, affine normalization to $[0, 1]$ incurs a penalty on the confidence boundary width. As a consequence, the empirical reduction in time-to-alarm over pure SRM is sometimes modest (e.g., ~760 vs. ~790 steps in Fig. 2(b), ~500 vs. ~530 steps in Fig. 3).

Discussion of hyperparameter $\eta_{\max}$: Section 3.2 relies on an affine normalization with a maximum permitted parameter $\eta_{\max}$ to keep the scaled loss within $[0, 1]$. The sensitivity to $\eta_{\max}$ and guidelines for choosing it in practice should be more prominently discussed in the main text.

Restriction to bounded loss functions: The methodology relies on bounded loss functions (such as 0-1 loss or squared Brier score) due to the underlying martingale concentration inequalities. Extensions or limitations regarding unbounded losses (e.g., cross-entropy/log-loss) are not addressed.

strengths: Principled and statistically sound framework: The paper provides a rigorous semi-supervised extension of Supervised Risk Monitoring (SRM) by integrating Prediction-Powered Inference (PPI). By ensuring the shrinkage/tuning parameters {\eta_t} form a predictable sequence, the estimators remain unbiased and allow anytime-valid confidence bounds via the conjugate-mixture empirical Bernstein inequality with distribution-free type-I error guarantees.

Practical and well-motivated setting: Purely supervised monitoring requires continuous true label feedback which is prohibitive in practice, whereas purely unsupervised methods rely on unverified calibration assumptions. PPRM effectively bridges this gap by leveraging abundant unlabeled data with a minimal labeled stream.

Adaptive variance reduction mechanism: The online adaptive estimation of \eta_t via a sliding window empirically and theoretically protects against uninformative or poorly calibrated auxiliary predictors fp(\cdot), gracefully retreating toward supervised performance rather than corrupting the bounds.

Thorough and diverse experimental validation: The paper tests across distinct real-world applications (computer vision on CIFAR-10-C, LLM QA evaluation across multiple open/closed judges, and telecommunication MIMO channel equalization), and includes extensive analyses on empirical false alarm rates, abrupt shifts, intermittent label streams, and window size sensitivity.
weaknesses: Range normalization penalty: Because the PPI estimator takes values in [-\eta_t, 1 + \eta_t], affine normalization into [0, 1] introduces a (1 + 2\eta)^2 scaling penalty into the variance and boundary width (as analyzed in Proposition A.1). While this trade-off is investigated in Appendix A.4, the discussion in the main paper (Section 3.2) is brief regarding when this penalty outweighs the variance reduction benefits.

Synchronous label availability assumption: The main theoretical framework assumes at least one labeled observation is available at every discrete time step t (n_t >= 1). In many practical streaming scenarios, true labels arrive with arbitrary feedback delays or in sporadic batches; while Appendix D.4 introduces an intermittent formulation, it relies on proxy bounds (Assumption B.1) from unsupervised monitoring rather than an assumption-free delayed-label martingale formulation.

Comparison with prediction-powered e-detectors: While the authors briefly contrast their work with Csillag et al. (2025) and test-martingale change-point detection (e-detectors), an empirical comparison against testing-by-betting e-detector baselines under identical shift conditions would provide further insight into the trade-offs between tracking cumulative running risk versus instantaneous changepoint detection.

strengths: Principled and statistically sound framework: The paper provides a rigorous extension of Supervised Risk Monitoring (SRM) to the semi-supervised regime using Prediction-Powered Inference (PPI). The reliance on a predictable sequence of hyperparameters {\eta_t} neatly guarantees that the risk estimators remain conditionally unbiased, ensuring exact finite-sample Type-I error control via time-uniform empirical Bernstein confidence sequences without requiring assumptions on the surrogate predictor.

Well-characterized theoretical trade-offs: Section 3.3 and Appendix A.4 clearly articulate the trade-off between variance reduction (from positive covariance between surrogate and true losses) and the range-expansion penalty incurred when normalizing the PPI estimate into [0, 1], yielding concrete conditions (Proposition A.1) under which PPRM provably accelerates detection.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: The method is validated across a diverse set of tasks—including vision (CIFAR-10-C), multimodal LLM evaluation (QA benchmarks using both open-weight and proprietary models as judges), and a telecommunications channel equalization problem—accompanied by thorough ablations on window sizes, intermittent labeling, and predictor quality.
weaknesses: Incremental methodological novelty: The core contribution is a straightforward synthesis of two existing paradigms: Supervised Risk Monitoring with empirical Bernstein confidence sequences (Podkopaev & Ramdas, 2022) and PPI / PPI++ variance reduction (Angelopoulos et al., 2023a,b). The derivation largely follows standard predictable sequence arguments and plug-in variance minimization.

Requirement of immediate, synchronous labels: The primary formulation assumes access to at least n_t >= 1 ground-truth label at every single monitoring round t. In practical streaming deployments, ground-truth feedback often arrives with substantial delay (label lag) or irregularly. While Appendix D.4 considers intermittent labels, that extension relies on the proxy-based assumptions of Schirmer et al. (2025), forfeiting the assumption-free guarantee of the main method.

Modest detection speedups versus auxiliary model overhead: In several benchmark settings, the practical reduction in time to alarm over standard SRM is modest (e.g., in Figure 2(a), ~760 steps for PPRM vs. ~800 for SRM; in Figure 3, ~500 vs. ~530). When the auxiliary predictor is computationally expensive (such as querying GPT-4 or large vision-language models), the operational cost of maintaining and querying the surrogate predictor continuously may outweigh the marginal gain in detection latency.

Lack of analysis regarding the range hyperparameter \eta_max: The affine normalization g_a(\cdot) in Section 3.2 requires fixing a global upper bound \eta_max in advance. Because the width of the confidence sequence depends directly on the normalization interval [-\eta_max, 1 + \eta_max], the sensitivity of the lower bounds and detection times to the choice of \eta_max is an important practical factor that is left unanalyzed.

strengths: Practical and well-motivated problem: deployed models inevitably face distribution shifts, and while supervised risk monitoring requires costly ground-truth feedback, fully unsupervised methods rely on strong, unverifiable calibration assumptions. The proposed semi-supervised setting with prediction-powered inference is a natural and appealing middle ground.

Rigorously preserved anytime validity: by ensuring that the tuning parameter $\eta_t$ is chosen in a predictable manner (using only historical data up to $t-1$), the prediction-powered risk estimate remains conditionally unbiased, enabling the valid application of time-uniform concentration bounds (CM-EB) without heuristic approximations.

Comprehensive and diverse evaluation across vision benchmarks (CIFAR-10-C), modern LLM question-answering pipelines (using various open- and closed-source judge LLMs), and a realistic wireless channel equalization scenario.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the methodological contribution is essentially an assembly of existing techniques—sequential risk monitoring with CM-EB confidence sequences (Podkopaev & Ramdas, 2021; Howard et al., 2021), prediction-powered inference with variance-minimizing control variates (Angelopoulos et al., 2023a,b), and betting-based confidence bounds (Waudby-Smith & Ramdas, 2024; Einbinder et al., 2025).

Missing empirical evaluation of false alarm rates: while Theorem 3.2 provides theoretical PFA guarantees, the empirical section completely lacks experiments verifying empirical false alarm control under the null hypothesis ($H_0$, stationary or benign non-harmful shift). Given that sequential bounds can often be overly conservative, assessing whether the test exhausts its budget $\delta$ under $H_0$ is essential.

Modest empirical reduction in detection delay: the empirical speedup over standard supervised risk monitoring (SRM) is relatively minor across tasks (e.g., in Figure 2(a), PPRM triggers at $t \approx 760$ vs. SRM at $t \approx 800$; in Figure 2(b), $\approx 760$ vs. $\approx 790$; in Figure 3(b), $\approx 500$ vs. $\approx 530$). The error bars and distributions overlap considerably, raising questions about whether the practical benefit justifies maintaining an auxiliary predictor and unlabeled pipeline.

Unaddressed scaling penalty in confidence bounds: because the PPI estimator $\hat{R}_t^{PP}$ takes values in $[-\eta_t, \eta_t + 1]$, the loss must undergo an affine transformation into $[0, 1]$ scaled by $(1 + 2\eta_{\max})$. The paper does not analyze or document how sensitive the empirical Bernstein width is to the choice of $\eta_{\max}$, which inherently inflates the bound width and can counteract the variance reduction benefits of unlabeled data.

strengths: Principled and statistically sound framework: The paper successfully adapts Prediction-Powered Inference (PPI) to sequential risk monitoring, using predictable hyperparameter updates to preserve the martingale/anytime-valid property of empirical Bernstein confidence sequences.

Rigorously proven finite-sample guarantees: PPRM provides assumption-free control of the probability of false alarm (PFA) without relying on heuristic calibration or strong assumptions regarding the accuracy of the surrogate predictor.

Practical and well-motivated setting: The semi-supervised setup directly addresses the real-world dilemma between label scarcity (which hinders Supervised Risk Monitoring) and lack of formal guarantees/low power (which plagues Unsupervised Risk Monitoring).

Diverse and convincing experimental evaluation: Evaluated across three distinct application domains (vision with CIFAR-10-C, NLP with multiple LLM-as-a-judge QA benchmarks, and wireless communications), showing consistent reductions in detection delay compared to supervised and unsupervised baselines.

Helpful ablation studies: The paper clearly evaluates the impact of surrogate model capability (from small local models up to GPT-4.1) as well as the benefit of adaptive variance-minimizing weighting (η_t).
weaknesses: Missing empirical validation of false alarm rates under H_0: While Theorem 3.2 guarantees PFA <= delta, the paper only reports detection times under distribution shift (H_1). Empirical false alarm rates under nominal conditions (where no shift occurs or shift is strictly within epsilon_tol) should be reported to verify empirical conservativeness.

Omission of analysis on eta_max and the rescaling penalty: Bounding R^{PP}_t into [0, 1] requires scaling by (1 + 2*eta_max), which widens the resulting confidence sequence. The paper does not specify the exact value of eta_max used in experiments nor analyze how sensitive detection speed is to this truncation boundary.

Cost and resource overhead discussion: In settings like the LLM QA task, running an auxiliary LLM (such as GPT-4.1) on N_t = 15 unlabeled samples at every time step incurs significant computational and financial costs. A discussion of the compute/label-cost Pareto frontier would enhance practical relevance.

Inherent inertia of running risk: Monitoring the cumulative average running risk R_bar_t is robust but exhibits significant inertia if a sudden shift occurs at a large time t. While inherited from Podkopaev & Ramdas (2021), a brief discussion contrasting running-risk monitoring with instantaneous change-point detection would add clarity.

strengths: Principled and practical formulation: The paper effectively addresses a key limitation in sequential risk monitoring—namely, the scarcity and cost of online ground-truth labels—by establishing a semi-supervised monitoring framework combining Prediction-Powered Inference (PPI) and anytime-valid confidence sequences.

Rigorous statistical guarantees: By ensuring that the tuning parameter sequence {\eta_t} is predictable via historical sliding-window estimation, the proposed PPRM method maintains finite-sample, assumption-free control of the probability of false alarm (PFA) without requiring assumptions on the accuracy or calibration of the auxiliary predictor.

Adaptive variance minimization: The paper derives the closed-form one-step optimal value \eta_t^* for the sequential setting, and demonstrates empirically (Table 1) that adaptive estimation noticeably speeds up detection compared to a fixed hyperparameter choice.

Diverse and realistic experimental validation: The method is validated across three distinct application domains (vision with ResNet on CIFAR-10-C, LLM-as-a-judge QA monitoring with open and closed models, and MIMO wireless channel equalization), demonstrating consistent reductions in time-to-alarm compared to supervised (SRM) and unsupervised (URM) baselines.
weaknesses: Incremental algorithmic novelty: The core methodological contribution is largely a combination of existing frameworks—specifically, applying PPI++ estimators (Angelopoulos et al., 2023b) inside the anytime-valid empirical Bernstein confidence sequences of SRM (Howard et al., 2021; Podkopaev & Ramdas, 2021).

Range inflation tradeoff from affine normalization: Because \hat{R}_t^{PP} falls in [-\eta_t, 1 + \eta_t], normalizing it to [0, 1] requires scaling by (1 + 2\eta_{max}). This widens the effective range of the bounded variable, which can inflate the concentration term u(V_t^{PP})/t unless the variance reduction from unlabeled data is sufficiently large. A deeper theoretical or empirical discussion on the choice and sensitivity of \eta_{max} is missing.

Lack of empirical PFA validation under the null hypothesis: While time-to-alarm under harmful shift (H_1) is well documented across scenarios, the paper does not report empirical false alarm frequencies under nominal/stationary conditions (H_0) to demonstrate how conservative the theoretical bound (\delta_S + \delta_T) is in practice.
